latestPosts.caption: My hope for the future? That every woman—no matter who she is or where she lives—can step into her full power because she’s able to get the care she needs.

If you want proof that our health systems overlook women, just look at menopause. It affects half the population, yet it remains poorly understood and drastically underfunded, leaving women without the care and relief they need. 
 
In The New York Times, I share why I’m directing new funding to raise the standard of care for menopause and perimenopause—and what it will take to unlock a menopause revolution. Read the full piece at the link in my bio.

Unlocking women’s power changes everything.
 
In our homes. 
In our workplaces. 
In our communities. 
In the rooms where laws are passed. 
And at the tables where decisions are made.

“I want every good thing for this child before I have another.” A mom named Marianne told me that when I was in Kenya in 2011, and it’s stuck with me ever since. Every parent, no matter where they live, wants the chance to give their children the best possible start in life. On #WorldContraceptionDay, let’s remember that starts with something fundamental: the ability to decide whether and when to have children.

A journalist raising questions about lung cancer rates in women. A doctor who nearly became a maternal mortality statistic. A columnist shining a spotlight on menopause.  
 
These leaders are using their voices and platforms to highlight the distinct health challenges half the population faces.  
 
Today I’m sharing eight key voices for information and inspiration. I’d love to hear what you’d add to this list. Who and what have you been listening to, reading, or watching lately to learn more about women’s health?

I’ve heard from women all over the world how important it is to be able to decide for themselves whether and when to have children.

That’s why it’s essential that they have access to contraceptives and reliable information about their options. Their health and their families’ futures depend on it. #WorldContraceptionDay

"@melindafrenchgates, welcome to #NiceTalk!" 👏  Last week, the @pivotaldotcom founder joined @nikkiogun for a candid conversation around the intersection of women's health and power. 

Stay tuned for the full episode, coming soon. 👀

When we think about the stakes in healthcare, we tend to think of them in terms of life and death, being sick or being healthy. The conversation is about your physical well-being and maybe your mental health — and it pretty much stops there.

But your health impacts so much more, especially for women, a new survey from Gallup and Pivotal, a philanthropic group founded by Melinda French Gates, shows.

“Women are often taught to put themselves last and minimize their own needs,” Melinda wrote to Vox in an email. “They don’t always have time to care for themselves because they’re so busy caring for others. And they might not be able to afford childcare or home health support for their aging parents. Our survey showed one in six women delayed healthcare because of their responsibilities caring for their family members. For Black women it’s one in five, and Hispanic women one in four. Too many women are facing an uphill road to even just get to a doctor’s office.” 

“It’s possible to make it easier for people to balance healthcare and family responsibilities — but it’s going to take action from many angles. That’s exactly why I invest in both women’s health and in caregiving, and I’d encourage more philanthropists to do the same.”

Read more about why we need to invest more in women’s health — and how to accomplish it — at the link in our bio.

📸: Courtesy of Pivotal Ventures

More than 50% of U.S. women have had a negative experience seeking healthcare in the last five years. And 42% said their health has limited their careers.  
 
When women can’t get the care they need, it impacts every aspect of their lives. 
 
@pivotaldotcom partnered with @gallup to conduct one of the most expansive surveys on women’s health and opportunity ever fielded.  
What we found was that, for women, barriers to care too often become barriers to opportunity.  
 
Learn more about our findings on Pivotal.com

From hot flashes to night sweats, menopause comes with a long list of things women are told to brace for. Far less discussed is what menopause can cost a woman at work.

A major new survey from @pivotaldotcom, @melindafrenchgates, and Gallup quantifies that cost—and data shared exclusively with Marie Claire shows just how unevenly it falls. Women with the least financial cushion are absorbing the steepest career costs.

Tap the link in our bio to read more.

Women’s health is too important for any one group to tackle alone. That’s why I’m calling on business leaders, policymakers, philanthropists, care providers, and advocates to use their influence to improve women’s health.

Every so often, I read a book that stays with me long after I’ve finished it.  
 
“We Are Called to Rise: The Power of Refugee Women” by Jina Krause-Vilmar is one of those books, and I’m thrilled that it’s officially out today! 
 
It’s a powerful and thought-provoking read, and I’m so proud that it’s the next title from Moment of Lift Books. You can learn more about it—and get your copy—at MomentofLift.com linked in my bio.

Today is American Business Women’s Day, and I keep thinking about how recently women could be required to have a man’s signature to get a business loan.

Some states still required women to have a husband or other male relative co-sign a business loan until 1988?! What?! That was only 12 years before I started @spanx.

The progress came in steps. In 1974, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act made it illegal to deny women credit or require a male co-signer simply because they were women. Then, in 1988, the Women’s Business Ownership Act eliminated state laws requiring a husband or other male relative to co-sign a woman’s business loan - and expanded support for women entrepreneurs.

Not that long ago, a woman’s ability to access credit could depend on a man’s signature instead of her own ambition and ability to build. 🤯

Think of all the businesses, ideas, and inventions that may not have had the chance to exist before then.

I’m a big believer that the more women-owned businesses we have in this world, the better. ❤️

We give ourselves health checks. Our planet deserves one too.

Today, while in New York for Climate Week, I joined the Planetary Guardians and the brilliant Professor Johan Rockström to launch the 2026 Planetary Health Check, an annual scientific assessment of the systems that keep our Earth healthy.

The news is confronting. Seven of the planet’s nine safety boundaries have now been crossed, and all seven are moving in the wrong direction.

This isn’t some distant problem happening to somebody else. We feel it through hotter days, rising food prices, polluted air, floods, fires and droughts. It affects all of us.

But it’s not all doom and gloom - there are real reasons for hope. Solar power is doubling roughly every three years. One in four new cars sold worldwide is electric. And investment in clean energy is now nearly twice that going into fossil fuels.

The solutions are here. Now we need to use them at speed and scale to get our planet back into a safe space.

I want my grandchildren, and yours, to inherit a world every bit as beautiful as the one we’ve been lucky enough to enjoy.

Read the Planetary Health Check, share its findings and add your name to the call for planetary health to sit at the heart of global decision-making. This issue isn’t bigger than any of us, because every one of us can help.

What a beautiful story of hope in The @Guardian. Twenty-one years ago, a field in Norfolk was home to a single crop. Today, it is a wildflower meadow with more than 150 plant species. Since 2011, the only maintenance has been one hay cut each summer. The cut keeps the field from becoming woodland and gives more delicate wildflowers room to grow.

As @UCL Professor Carl Sayer put it: “Sometimes we’re not patient enough.” And after watching the meadow become more biodiverse each year, he says, “It’s hope — we can recover things. We just need to do less in the recovery process.”

Life is a dance between making it happen and letting it happen. In this meadow, making it happen means one simple act of care each year. Letting it happen means trusting nature and giving it time. The same is true in our lives: our daily choices around sleep, food, movement, stress and connection give our bodies and minds the support they need to renew.

Looking back at two great days at @Dreamforce. @Salesforce’s chief marketing officer @ErinOles moderated a conversation with @officiallymcconaughey and me about who shapes culture in the age of AI.

Here’s what nobody wants to admit about the content explosion: the bottleneck was never production. It was always judgment. For most of history, we assumed the hard part was making things — and the machines have now solved that. Anyone can generate a screenplay, a song, a strategy deck in seconds. But Matthew put his finger on what the machines haven’t solved: AI can tell you what’s popular, but it doesn’t yet have an ear for what’s really good.

Those are profoundly different things. Popularity is a pattern in the data. Good is a judgment — and judgment is built from everything that never shows up in training data: taste formed over decades, failures metabolized into instinct, the thousand small refinements of a lived life. Erin compressed it into one line: the real AI superpower isn’t the tool, it’s the taste.

Which means we’ve been worried about the wrong scarcity. The scarce resource of this era isn’t intelligence — machines have made intelligence abundant. It’s wisdom. And here’s the inconvenient truth about wisdom: it can’t be generated, downloaded, or scaled. It has to be lived into existence, one experience at a time.

Machines gather knowledge exponentially. Humans gather wisdom slowly. Whether that gap becomes a crisis or a renaissance depends entirely on whether we treat our own development as seriously as we treat the technology’s. And keeping people at the center of the AI conversation was the focus of my session at Dreamforce with chief people officer Nathalie Scardino and HR leaders from around the world.

A beautiful evening celebrating the opening of the @LucasMuseum of Narrative Art — a museum as expansive, surprising and impossible to categorize as the works it celebrates.

The museum houses the art collection of George Lucas and @MellodyHobson. At a time when AI dominates our public conversation, it’s a reminder that machines aren’t the only ones producing wonders. It’s a cathedral of wonder and awe, human creativity, storytelling and connection. As Mellody said, “Narrative art creates an emotional connection, not an intellectual one.”

The museum looks, appropriately, like a spaceship, rising, curving and folding into the landscape – in fact, there isn’t a right angle anywhere in the building. Works associated with empires and religious traditions live alongside illustrations, comic strips and movie images that have shaped our lives. There is even an immersive reproduction of the Sistine Chapel ceiling, which George calls “God’s comic book” because its panels tell a story. And throughout, cinema is treated not as something separate from art history but as another chapter in our ancient drive to turn experience into narrative. It’s why one of the museum’s theaters is named for Robert Flaherty, a pioneer of documentary filmmaking.

And then there are the monsters. The museum’s exploration of them brought to mind what Guillermo del Toro’s work shows about monsters being revealing mirrors. We create them to give form to what frightens us and to explore the parts of ourselves we can’t always confront directly. The same is true of the myths, which let us wrestle with the same big questions at a larger scale. The characters and settings change but the elemental questions remain: Who are we? What do we fear? What are we willing to fight for? And who can we become?

At a moment when so much is pulling us apart, George Lucas and Mellody Hobson have created a home for the images, stories and myths that unite us — a place where art is an invitation to feel, wonder and see ourselves in one another.

As we mark World Alzheimer’s Day, more than 7 million people over age 65 in the US are living with Alzheimer’s disease — a figure that is projected to almost double in the next few decades. And more than 12 million people are caregivers to loved ones with Alzheimer’s or other dementias. There’s no sugarcoating a disease that results in the widespread loss of brain function, and no number that captures the heartbreak of seeing a loved one decline. And yet, there is reason for hope.

That’s because research shows that Alzheimer’s-related brain changes can begin up to 20 years before symptoms set in, highlighting the importance of investing in our brain health and addressing modifiable risk factors throughout adulthood.

This is a 20-year window of opportunity. As with so many chronic conditions, research is showing that with brain health, our DNA is not necessarily our destiny. We have more power than we previously thought to shape our brain health, both day-to-day and in the long run.

Read more in @incmagazine at the link in bio.

Thursday evening on brain health was the largest event I’ve ever had in my home. And it so perfectly captured the sense of possibility of this moment, when brain health has moved from medical journals to the center of the conversation on health. I moderated a wide-ranging conversation with Andrew Adams, Group VP of Molecule Discovery, Lilly Research Laboratories, who shared not only about his work on molecular discovery and genetic medicines, but how it is inspired by the lived experience of his mother and grandmother; Konstantina Stankovic, the chair of otolaryngology and head and neck surgery at @Stanford Medicine, who urged us to “protect our senses,” since our hearing, smell and other senses are key inputs to the brain and some of the first signals that can tell us when an intervention is needed; and Baba Shiv, a behavioral neuroscientist and professor at the @StanfordGSB, who shared that when multitasking and distraction are taking such a toll on our brain health, one of the best Microsteps we can take is to “learn how to subtract before you can add.”

It was a great conversation, and one of the themes that emerged was that with brain health, the biggest innovations are being driven not by competitive advantage but “collaborative advantage.”

And the collective wisdom in the room proved it. As we opened the floor to questions and comments, we heard from authors (neurologist @teenashettymd, whose Healing the Brain came out earlier this month, and Sandro Galea, Dean at the School of Public Health at Washington University in St. Louis and author most recently of Why Health?), entrepreneurs (Shiv Rao, CEO and co-founder of AI health company Abridge), and clinicians including Dr. David Dodick, Chief Medical Officer at the Atria Health and Research Institute, and Brendan G. Carr, the CEO of Mount Sinai Health System.

New research from @gallup and @pivotaldotcom quantifies what women have been reporting for years: women face significant barriers in getting healthcare, and these barriers affect more than just health outcomes.

51% of women report at least one negative experience with healthcare providers — symptoms dismissed, misdiagnosis, or not getting needed answers. For men, it’s 39%.

The findings also make clear that the consequences extend well beyond health outcomes. 54% of women report an impact on family life or relationships, 42% on work or career, and 32% on community participation.
That’s the reframe this research offers: barriers to care are not only a health problem. They’re a barrier to opportunity, with effects that ripple through families, workplaces, communities, and our economy.

Women are accomplishing so much despite these barriers. Imagine the possibilities — for their health, their connections, and so much more — if they got the care they needed.

Yesterday afternoon at @Dreamforce with @Salesforce President and Chief People Officer Nathalie Scardino and a group of people leaders talking about AI, work, and what it means to be irreplaceably human.

AI is now saving managers nearly three hours per week. But 36% of them say they waste more than half of it.

It’s called the AI Efficiency Trap — when productivity gains create pressure to simply do more, feeding the very stress and burnout the technology was supposed to relieve. 

Avoiding that trap is the real opportunity for leaders — and it’s much bigger than deploying new tools. It’s being intentional about the time AI gives back: reinvesting it in recharging, in creativity, in connection, in the work that requires our full attention and judgment. And it’s making clear to your people that their value is measured not in additional output for its own sake, but in their capacity to think, create and connect.

The companies that thrive in this era won’t be defined by how much time AI saved them, but by how deliberately they reinvested it.

5 one-month challenges that can change your life:
(Save this for progress!)

1. The communication challenge.

For the next 30 days, record yourself for one minute. 
Watch the video. Note down the mistakes. 
The next day, try to improve them.

2. The ‘saying no’ challenge. 

The things you often say yes to - to your boss, your parents, your friends - slowly practice saying no.

For 30 days, say no at least once every day in a situation where you used to say yes.

3. The decision-making challenge.

Whenever you have to make an important decision, give yourself a 10-minute timer. 
You must take a decision in 10 minutes.

Within 30 days, your capacity to take decisions under pressure will increase.

4. The negotiation challenge.

At least once a week, ask for a better deal. Negotiate. Ask for a better price.

In the beginning, you face humiliation. 
It feels very awkward. 
By the 30th day, you have a lot more confidence.

5. The structured thinking challenge.

Whenever you think about a problem, write it down. 
Break it down.

With small problems, the more you do that, the more structure enters the way you think.

Which one are you starting today?

⁣
⁣I’ve been getting a lot of DMs and texts (yes, I text back: 323-591-5921) from recent graduates who are feeling a little lost. I want you to know that you’re not alone. You’re entering a world and a workforce during a time that is more uncertain and more confusing than anyone alive has experienced. ⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣You may be having trouble finding a job. You may have gotten a job and lost it or found it delayed. You may be figuring out what your next move should be. It may feel like the pressure is on to be a star.  To be precocious. To be not only accomplished—but accomplished for your age.⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣I’m here to tell you to stop. Because the world has stopped. Any expectations you may have had just a few short months ago need to change. Consider this an opportunity to delay adulthood. A delay the rest of us we wish we all had. ⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣The truth is, you’re going to work for the rest of your life. It may seem glamorous to have a job or to build your resume or to start a business. And it’s great, sure. It gives us a sense of purpose. It builds our future.⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣But the future is coming slower than any of us could’ve imagined and we must slow down to keep pace. If you’re not getting the job you want, remember that nobody gives a shit about your first job. Your resume is a big experiment right now and that’s OK.⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣This is carte blanche permission to take a break—because you just accomplished something really huge. It’ll be a while before you accomplish anything remotely as huge. Hell, you may never even keep a job for four years. ⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣If you’re able to live with your parents right now, consider it a blessing. The rush to adulthood is a scam. Get existential. Don’t prioritize independence over the opportunity to spend rich, quality time with those you love. Because you probably won’t do it when you only get two weeks of paid time off a year. ⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣It’s the best time in your life to fuck off, so take advantage. 🌻
